name: Facial lifting tape

lead: Facial lifting tape consists of adhesive strips or invisible patches stuck to the cheeks, jawline or temples and pulled backward, usually hidden under hair or clothing. People use it for an immediately tighter-looking face, with softer jowls and lines, for photos, film and events.

The lift is mechanical: the adhesive holds skin in a different position for as long as it is worn, a styling trick with a long history in photography, film and event work. It does not claim to change skin structure, and published research on facial taping covers other uses, such as elastic therapeutic tape for swelling after facial fracture surgery and rehabilitation for Bell's palsy.

paras: Users place the strips along the hairline or behind the ears, pull the skin back and secure them under hair, then apply makeup and style over the top. It is applied for the occasion, and the effect ends when the tape comes off.

Reported drawbacks are skin irritation, adhesive reactions and redness on removal, and sleeping in it can leave marks. People with sensitive skin or adhesive allergies are usually advised to patch test.

chain: Tighter-looking face for photos or events
angle.text: Tape pulls the cheeks and jaw back for an instant, taut-looking face in photos, film and at events. The lift is mechanical and lasts while the tape is on.

lead: Facial lifting tape consists of adhesive strips or clear patches that are stuck to the cheeks, jawline or temples and pulled back, usually hidden under hair, to make sagging skin look tighter and the jawline and cheekbones look more defined. People use it for photographs, filming and events because the change is visible immediately and needs no procedure. The practice has a long history in photography, film and event styling.

The lift is mechanical: the adhesive holds the skin in a different position while the tape is worn, so the effect is expected to end when the tape comes off. No published study has examined cosmetic lifting tape for skin structure or lasting effect. Published research on facial taping concerns other uses, including elastic therapeutic tape for swelling after facial fracture surgery and taping as part of rehabilitation for Bell's palsy.[1][2]

For context, surgical facelifts (rhytidectomy) have a history stretching back to about 1901, and Wikipedia describes skin-only facelifts as lasting roughly five to ten years, with costs in the thousands of dollars; tape is positioned by users as a short-term, low-cost alternative for specific occasions.[3] Reported drawbacks of tape include skin irritation and adhesive reactions.

paras: Products include clear or skin-tone adhesive patches, pre-cut strips with a pull-tab and elastic bands attached to medical-grade tape. The user places the adhesive on the skin of the cheek or jaw, pulls the loose end toward the hairline or behind the ear and fixes it, and conceals the ends with hair. Stylists and makeup artists have used such techniques for decades.

Lifting tape works by direct traction on the skin. It does not stimulate collagen or change tissue, so any change in appearance lasts only as long as the tape stays in place. A separate category, elastic therapeutic (kinesio) tape, is applied in sports and rehabilitation medicine, where proponents claim effects on swelling and circulation; one 2018 randomized study of 28 men found that applying kinesio tape with wrinkles (convolutions) on the lower back did not increase skin temperature, which the authors used as a proxy for local circulation.[4]
No studies found of adhesive facial lifting tape for cosmetic skin lifting or anti-aging.

subs.h: Related research on taping of the face
paras: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials (319 participants) examined elastic therapeutic tape after surgery for facial fractures. Only two trials were suitable for pooling edema data, and the authors concluded that tape appeared effective for controlling postoperative edema, with unclear effects on pain and trismus and a high risk of bias in the included studies.[1]

A randomized study of 20 patients with Bell's palsy examined facial taping as a biofeedback aid alongside Kabat rehabilitation, and reported greater improvement in palsy severity scores in the taping group than with rehabilitation alone.[2] These applications address swelling or neuromuscular rehabilitation rather than cosmetic lifting.

Adhesives can cause contact irritation, allergic reactions and redness or stripping of the skin on removal, and wearing tape overnight or for long periods can leave marks. No studies have quantified these risks for cosmetic lifting tape.

Lifting tape is discussed as an instant, low-cost way to look more defined for photographs or events, and some users also apply tape at night in the hope of lasting effects. Whether overnight use has any lasting effect has not been studied.

Wikipedia's article on rhytidectomy traces the surgical facelift from 1901 and describes later developments such as SMAS-layer techniques (1976) and deep plane and volumetric approaches. It reports that skin-only facelifts can last about five to ten years and that recovery for a traditional facelift is around three to four weeks.[3]

The same article lists non-surgical options including thread lifts, which it describes as using barbed threads to pull skin upward; it quotes physician Vincent Wong in a 2021 BBC report calling thread lifts the most dangerous procedure an aesthetic practitioner can do. It does not discuss tape.[3] Tape differs from these in that it involves no tissue change and is fully reversible.

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer reportedly performs the first facelift in Berlin.[3]
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS layer, shaping modern facelift techniques.[3]
Randomized study of facial taping as biofeedback in Bell's palsy published.[2]
Meta-analysis of elastic therapeutic tape after facial fracture surgery published.[1]
